cons.claim: Visible effort creates the impression that the advisor controls outcomes they do not control, and the client's disappointment attaches to the advisor rather than the carrier
cons.example: a client who blames the advisor for a hotel category the operator substituted under a contractual right

failure_modes: improvising a fix and buying replacement services before establishing what the responsible party owes
letting the traveler accept the first offer without knowing what it forecloses
going quiet while working, so the client escalates emotionally
handling everything by phone and leaving no timestamped record for the claim afterwards
acceptance_tests: each incident has a log with timestamps, the contractual owner of the fix, actions attempted, names and supplier responses, and the notification cadence actually met
the file shows the client was told plainly which parts of the situation were outside the advisor's control
revisit_triggers: a disruption is resolved, which should trigger a review of what the protocol handled badly
a supplier's escalation path fails during a live incident
the same failure class recurs across clients

base.update_signal: a live incident exposes a step that made things worse, or a supplier escalation route that no longer works

nodes.definition: Pursuing remedy after a documented service failure - a category not delivered, a cancelled excursion, a substituted property, a transfer that never arrived - without ever promising the client an outcome. The advisor assembles the evidence trail already built by reconciliation and the incident log, files with the supplier through its own claims channel with a specific and proportionate ask rather than a general complaint, escalates factually up the relationship path when the first response is inadequate, and keeps the client informed about what is realistically available: a partial refund, a credit, a goodwill gesture, or sometimes nothing. Part of the skill is routing correctly - some failures belong to a carrier's own compensation regime and some to a protection policy's claims process, which the client pursues with the advisor supplying documentation rather than interpreting coverage. The honest framing throughout is that the advisor will press hard and prove the facts, but does not decide the result.

included: evidence assembly and proportionate claim construction
factual escalation through the supplier and relationship path
routing claims to the correct regime or process
honest expectation-setting about achievable remedy classes
excluded: interpreting insurance policy coverage or advising on a claim's merits
legal action or advice
promising or guaranteeing any compensation

pros.claim: A specific, evidenced and proportionate ask is answered far more often than an emotional complaint
pros.example: a claim citing the sold category, the confirmation and dated photographs, asking for the difference rather than for the trip to be made right

pros.claim: Visible advocacy after a failure is one of the strongest loyalty events available to an advisory practice, even when the recovery is partial
pros.example: a client who stays with the practice for years because of how a bad hotel was handled rather than because the trips were flawless

cons.claim: Pressing claims consumes unpaid hours and spends relationship capital that has other uses
cons.example: weeks of correspondence over a modest refund with an operator the practice books monthly

cons.claim: Clients often expect the advisor to deliver a remedy that the responsible party simply will not give, and the disappointment can land on the advisor
cons.example: a client who wanted the whole trip refunded for one poor night and reads a partial credit as the advisor failing

failure_modes: promising an outcome to calm a client and then failing to deliver it
filing a general complaint instead of a specific and evidenced ask
drifting into interpreting a protection policy's coverage for the client
letting the desire to protect a supplier relationship soften a legitimate claim
acceptance_tests: each claim on file names the specific failure, cites the sold-versus-delivered evidence, states a proportionate ask and records every response
no communication in the file promises a compensation outcome, and the achievable remedy classes were explained to the client in writing
revisit_triggers: a supplier refuses or ignores a documented claim
the same failure produces claims across multiple clients
a client escalates outside the practice

base.update_signal: claim outcomes cluster by supplier or by claim construction, showing which asks actually get answered

nodes.definition: The structured conversation after the client returns that harvests what actually happened and sorts it into the right bucket. The advisor asks specifically rather than generally - which base worked, which transfer was too tight, which guide was tired, what they would change, what surprised them - and then separates three different things that a happy or unhappy client will blend together: design error that belongs to the advisor, supplier failure that belongs to the ledger and possibly to a claim, and expectation mismatch that belongs to how the trip was described at proposal. Each finding is routed accordingly, so the design heuristics, the supplier record and the proposal language all improve from the same conversation. It is explicitly a quality-control instrument rather than a sales call: asking for a review, a referral or the next booking is a separate motion that happens later and belongs to the practice's client-retention discipline, not to this one.

included: specific structured questioning about the delivered trip
separating design error, supplier failure and expectation mismatch
routing each finding to design, ledger or proposal language
excluded: referral and review asks
anniversary or re-booking cadence and campaigns
valuing the client base

pros.claim: Sorting feedback into design, supplier and expectation buckets is what turns a pleasant chat into an improvement the next client can feel
pros.example: recognizing that a complaint about a rushed morning was a pacing decision by the advisor, not the operator's fault

pros.claim: A quality-first debrief that asks for nothing makes the later retention conversation easier because the client has already been heard
pros.example: a client who volunteers a recommendation unprompted because the debrief made clear the advisor wanted the truth

cons.claim: Clients soften negative feedback to be polite, so the debrief systematically under-reports problems unless questions are specific
cons.example: a party who says everything was lovely and mentions only in passing that they never used the second guide

cons.claim: Debriefs happen when the trip is over and the advisor is already working the next file, so they are the first thing dropped under pressure
cons.example: a busy season where three months of trips return with no debriefs recorded

failure_modes: asking how was the trip and accepting a one-word answer
recording feedback without attributing it to design, supplier or expectation
turning the debrief into a sales conversation and losing the honest answers
letting findings sit in notes without routing them anywhere
acceptance_tests: every completed trip has a debrief record, or an explicit note that the client declined one
each finding in the debrief is tagged as design, supplier or expectation and routed to the corresponding artifact
revisit_triggers: a client raises an issue after the debrief that the debrief did not surface
the same finding recurs across several trips
a supplier disputes a debrief finding attributed to them

base.update_signal: post-trip complaints arrive through other channels that the debrief should have caught, or debrief findings stop changing anything downstream

nodes.definition: The running, per-supplier record of delivered performance, kept as dated observations tied to specific bookings rather than as impressions. It tracks confirmation accuracy, whether what was sold is what arrived, on-the-ground quality and consistency, responsiveness when something broke and in whose time zone, honesty about problems rather than deflection, behavior on a redress claim, and payment and paperwork behavior toward the practice. Its purpose is to make future selection change on evidence: two documented failures on the same dimension should move a supplier down or off the shortlist regardless of how pleasant the relationship is, and a small operator that performed brilliantly under pressure should rise regardless of size. The ledger is the specific mechanism that stops a hosted lunch, a long friendship or a familiar brand from outweighing three bad client experiences.

included: dated per-booking performance observations
dimension-level tracking including disruption behavior and claim conduct
shortlist promotion and demotion rules driven by evidence
excluded: commission performance and payment amounts
supplier contract negotiation
public reviews or naming suppliers publicly

pros.claim: Dated, booking-linked evidence lets a supplier decision be defended to a client and to the advisor's own bias
pros.example: declining to recommend a familiar operator because the ledger shows three transfer failures in one season

pros.claim: The ledger converts scattered experience into a genuine practice asset that survives a bad memory or a busy season
pros.example: recalling instantly which of two similar operators actually answered during a strike two years ago

cons.claim: Small practices have thin per-supplier samples, so a single bad experience can unfairly condemn a good supplier
cons.example: one dreadful guide day recorded against an operator the practice has used only twice

cons.claim: Maintaining the ledger takes discipline at exactly the moment the trip is over and attention has moved on
cons.example: a season of trips whose observations were never written down and are now vague impressions

failure_modes: recording impressions rather than dated, booking-linked observations
letting relationship warmth override recorded failures
never demoting anyone, so the ledger accumulates without changing behavior
treating a single data point as a pattern
acceptance_tests: each entry names the booking, the date, the dimension and what was observed rather than a general rating
the shortlist used for selection reflects the ledger's current promotions and demotions
revisit_triggers: a supplier accumulates repeat failures on one dimension
a supplier changes ownership or key staff
a demoted supplier is proposed again for a specific client need

base.update_signal: accumulated entries change which supplier the practice would select for a repeat trip type, or a demoted supplier's new evidence contradicts the record

nodes.definition: Keeping the client record rich enough that the next trip starts from knowledge rather than from zero, while holding only what the work actually requires. The useful half is durable: preferences, pace, past bases and what they thought of them, celebration dates, loyalty numbers, seat and room habits, and the constraint history that makes a second design faster and better. The sensitive half is temporary: passport images and numbers, dates of birth, medical detail and any payment information are collected for a specific booking, held only as long as that booking needs them, protected under whatever data-protection obligation class applies in the practice's jurisdiction, and disposed of on a stated schedule rather than accumulating forever in an inbox. The steward's question is not whether something could be useful one day, but what would break if it leaked; the client's convenience is never a reason to keep an identity document longer than the booking requires.

included: durable preference and constraint history for future design
minimization, retention and disposal of sensitive identifiers
access discipline and protection appropriate to the practice's obligation class
excluded: legal advice on data-protection obligations, which must be verified against current rules in the jurisdiction
marketing consent management and campaign records
client-base valuation

pros.claim: A durable preference history is what makes a second trip feel effortless and is a genuine switching cost in the client's favor
pros.example: proposing a second itinerary that already accounts for the client's dislike of early flights and preference for a top-floor quiet room

pros.claim: Disposing of identity documents on schedule removes the practice's single largest breach exposure at no cost to service
pros.example: a compromised mailbox that contains no passport images because they were purged after each departure

cons.claim: Disposal costs convenience: the next booking has to ask for documents again, which clients experience as friction
cons.example: a repeat client irritated at re-sending passport details for the third trip in two years

cons.claim: Deciding what is durable versus sensitive requires judgment, and over-pruning loses context that made the practice valuable
cons.example: deleting the note explaining why a traveler cannot fly overnight along with the medical detail behind it

failure_modes: keeping passport images and card details indefinitely because they might be useful
storing sensitive detail in whatever channel it arrived in, including message threads
no retention schedule, so disposal never happens
treating a host's or supplier's system as covering an obligation the practice itself carries
acceptance_tests: sensitive identifiers have a stated retention period tied to the booking and evidence that disposal actually occurs
the durable client record contains preference and constraint history without carrying identity documents or payment data
the file names the data-protection obligation class the practice operates under and the date it was last verified
revisit_triggers: the practice changes systems, host or storage tooling
a data incident or near-miss occurs
the jurisdiction updates its data-protection requirement classes

base.update_signal: a data incident, a client access or deletion request, or a change in the jurisdiction's data-protection requirement classes
